title: MongoDB Driver Specifications: SDAM and Server Selection
objective: Frame the driver state-machine deep dive.
learnerQuestion: Why does a MongoDB driver need distributed-systems logic?
coreClaim: A MongoDB driver is a topology-aware client that discovers, monitors, selects, routes, and recovers across changing deployments.
mechanism: SDAM maintains topology state; server selection filters suitable servers per operation; CMAP and timeout specs determine whether selected servers are usable.
example: Replica set primary failover during writes and secondary reads.
counterpoint: Language drivers expose details differently, so check target driver docs for exact option names and defaults.
practicalTakeaway: Treat the driver as part of the distributed system.

title: What You Should Be Able To Reason About
learnerQuestion: What decisions should this deck help with?
coreClaim: Driver literacy helps tune discovery, read routing, timeouts, pooling, retries, and failure handling.
mechanism: Learning goals map hidden driver state to observable errors, options, and events.
example: Use server selection errors and driver events to debug failover.
counterpoint: Drivers hide complexity but do not remove the need for bounded application retries and observability.
practicalTakeaway: Tune from the operation path rather than isolated options.

title: A MongoDB Client Is Talking To A Moving Distributed System
learnerQuestion: What is the before-state without SDAM and server selection?
coreClaim: Replica set elections, stale seeds, network errors, sharded routers, and load balancers mean host strings are not enough.
mechanism: The driver converts changing server observations into a local topology map and per-operation target selection.
example: A primary steps down while writes are in flight.
counterpoint: The local map is eventually fresh, not omniscient.
practicalTakeaway: Expect temporary uncertainty during topology changes.

title: Three Driver Specs Work Together In Practice
objective: Connect SDAM, server selection, and CMAP/CSOT.
learnerQuestion: Which specs govern a single operation?
coreClaim: One operation crosses discovery state, server selection rules, timeout budgets, connection pools, retries, and command execution.
mechanism: SDAM feeds server selection; selection feeds pool checkout; timeout and retry rules bound the attempt.
example: A read waits for an eligible secondary, checks out a connection, and retries only if eligible.
counterpoint: Reading one spec in isolation can produce wrong tuning guidance.
practicalTakeaway: Debug operations across all relevant driver subsystems.

title: The Driver Keeps An Eventually Fresh Local Map
learnerQuestion: What does the driver know about the deployment?
coreClaim: Drivers maintain TopologyDescription and ServerDescription state from hello responses and errors.
mechanism: Server descriptions include type, RTT, tags, hosts, errors, and compatibility; topology description summarizes deployment type and suitable servers.
example: ReplicaSetNoPrimary during failover until a new primary is discovered.
counterpoint: The map can be stale between heartbeats or after network partitions.
practicalTakeaway: Read server selection errors as topology snapshots.

title: Drivers Route By Classified Server Type, Not By Host String
learnerQuestion: Why does a reachable host still not receive an operation?
coreClaim: A server must be classified as a suitable type for the operation and topology.
mechanism: Hello responses and SDAM rules classify Unknown, Standalone, Mongos, RSPrimary, RSSecondary, and related types.
example: A secondary is reachable but unsuitable for default primary reads and writes.
counterpoint: Direct connections intentionally change discovery assumptions.
practicalTakeaway: Reachability is not suitability.

title: The Topology State Machine Narrows Uncertainty Over Time
learnerQuestion: How does the driver move from unknown to known topology?
coreClaim: SDAM transitions topology state as it receives hello replies and errors.
mechanism: Unknown seeds become single, replica set, sharded, or load-balanced topology descriptions based on observations.
example: A seed host reports replica set membership and discovers other members.
counterpoint: Misconfigured set name or directConnection can constrain discovery.
practicalTakeaway: Connection string options shape what discovery is allowed to infer.

title: Background Heartbeats Keep The Topology Map Current
learnerQuestion: How does the driver notice changes?
coreClaim: Drivers monitor known servers with heartbeats and update descriptions from hello replies or failures.
mechanism: Heartbeat -> hello response/error -> RTT and server description update -> topology recomputation -> wake waiters.
example: Heartbeat discovers a new primary after election.
counterpoint: Heartbeat frequency trades freshness for monitoring overhead.
practicalTakeaway: Do not set heartbeat behavior without understanding detection latency.

title: The hello Response Is The State Machine's Input
learnerQuestion: What data drives topology decisions?
coreClaim: Hello replies provide server role, set membership, topology, wire version, and capability data.
mechanism: Drivers parse fields such as primary/writable state, hosts, setName, tags, maxWireVersion, and session timeout.
example: A secondary hello response can make it eligible for secondary read preference.
counterpoint: Incorrect hello metadata breaks driver decisions.
practicalTakeaway: Topology state is command-response driven.

title: A Seed List Is Only The Beginning
learnerQuestion: Why can the driver use hosts not listed in the URI?
coreClaim: Replica set discovery expands from seeds to members reported by hello responses.
mechanism: Driver connects to seeds, reads hosts/passives/arbiters, and updates known server list.
example: A URI with one seed discovers the full replica set.
counterpoint: DNS, SRV, TLS, set name, and network reachability still matter.
practicalTakeaway: Use seeds as entry points, not a static routing list.

title: The Driver Can Use A Set Even When The Seed List Is Stale
learnerQuestion: Can a driver recover from old host information?
coreClaim: Drivers can discover current replica set members from reachable seeds even if the seed list is incomplete or stale.
mechanism: SDAM replaces local descriptions with membership data reported by the deployment.
example: One old seed redirects the driver to current hosts through hello metadata.
counterpoint: If no seed is reachable or set names mismatch, discovery fails.
practicalTakeaway: Keep seeds healthy, but rely on discovery for membership updates.

title: Election Metadata Prevents Routing To An Old Primary
learnerQuestion: How does the driver avoid sending writes to an old primary?
coreClaim: Election metadata and topology updates invalidate stale primary descriptions.
mechanism: SDAM compares replica set version/election information and marks older primary observations stale.
example: During failover, the driver may report no primary rather than route incorrectly.
counterpoint: Temporary write unavailability is safer than stale primary routing.
practicalTakeaway: Failover errors can be correctness-preserving behavior.

title: Drivers May Monitor Differently, But Must Expose Equivalent Behavior
learnerQuestion: Do all drivers monitor exactly the same way?
coreClaim: Specifications require equivalent observable behavior even when implementation details differ.
mechanism: Drivers can use streaming or polling monitoring modes where supported while maintaining SDAM semantics.
example: A driver updates server descriptions from heartbeat responses regardless of monitoring implementation.
counterpoint: Event APIs and defaults vary by language driver.
practicalTakeaway: Rely on driver behavior contracts, but inspect language-specific observability.

title: Server Selection Turns Topology State Into One Operation Target
learnerQuestion: How does the driver pick exactly one server?
coreClaim: Server selection filters topology descriptions through operation requirements and routing policy.
mechanism: Topology type -> operation type -> read preference -> tags/staleness -> latency window -> pinning -> target.
example: A secondary read with tags first filters eligible secondaries, then applies latency window.
counterpoint: If no candidate remains, selection waits until timeout or topology changes.
practicalTakeaway: Debug selection by finding which filter removed candidates.

title: Normal Writes Require A Writable Target
learnerQuestion: Where do writes go?
coreClaim: Normal writes require a writable suitable server: typically replica set primary, mongos, or load-balanced target depending on topology.
mechanism: Server selection applies operation type and topology suitability rules.
example: A replica set with no known primary cannot select a write target.
counterpoint: Retryable writes and transactions add further eligibility and pinning rules.
practicalTakeaway: A write selection error often means no known writable server, not command failure.

title: Reads Are Routed By Explicit Policy
learnerQuestion: Why did a read go to that member?
coreClaim: Read routing follows read preference mode and optional tag, staleness, and latency rules.
mechanism: Modes include primary, primaryPreferred, secondary, secondaryPreferred, and nearest.
example: SecondaryPreferred can use a primary when no suitable secondary is available.
counterpoint: Secondary reads can be stale and may not match UX expectations.
practicalTakeaway: Set read preference per workload, not as a blanket scale setting.

title: Staleness And Tags Refine Secondary Eligibility
learnerQuestion: How can I constrain which secondaries are eligible?
coreClaim: Tag sets and maxStalenessSeconds narrow secondary candidates after read preference mode.
mechanism: Drivers filter servers by tag set order and staleness bounds defined by spec/manual behavior.
example: Read from region-tagged secondaries only if they are not too stale.
counterpoint: Too restrictive filters can leave no eligible server.
practicalTakeaway: Use tags/staleness to encode intent, then monitor candidate availability.

title: localThresholdMS Prevents Always Choosing The Absolute Fastest Ping
learnerQuestion: Why not always choose the lowest RTT server?
coreClaim: `localThresholdMS` creates a latency window among suitable servers.
mechanism: The driver keeps candidates whose RTT is within the fastest RTT plus the local threshold.
example: With default-like behavior, several nearby secondaries may be eligible instead of exactly one.
counterpoint: Setting localThresholdMS to zero can force lowest RTT but may reduce distribution.
practicalTakeaway: Tune latency windows for locality and distribution intentionally.

title: Some Operations Must Stay Pinned To Their Original Host
learnerQuestion: When is server selection not free to choose any eligible server?
coreClaim: Transactions, cursors/getMore, and load-balanced flows can pin operations to a host or connection.
mechanism: Driver state records selected server or connection for subsequent related operations.
example: A transaction remains associated with its selected server/connection context.
counterpoint: Pinning can concentrate load or fail if the pinned target disappears.
practicalTakeaway: Consider pinning when debugging uneven load or transaction errors.

title: Several Timeouts Control Different Parts Of The Path
learnerQuestion: Which timeout fired?
coreClaim: Server selection, operation budget, connection creation, socket I/O, pool checkout, and server execution are separate timing concerns.
mechanism: Different options and specs govern each stage before and during command execution.
example: A server selection timeout can occur before any command is sent.
counterpoint: Driver language versions may expose timeout behavior differently.
practicalTakeaway: Name the timed stage before changing a timeout.

title: serverSelectionTimeoutMS Is The Wait For A Suitable Server
learnerQuestion: What does serverSelectionTimeoutMS actually bound?
coreClaim: `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` bounds how long the driver waits to select a suitable server.
mechanism: Selection loops until a suitable server appears or the timeout expires.
example: During failover, writes wait for a known primary until selection timeout.
counterpoint: It is not the database command execution time.
practicalTakeaway: Tune selection timeout around failover tolerance and request deadlines.

title: timeoutMS Gives One Client-Side Operation Budget
learnerQuestion: How is timeoutMS different from serverSelectionTimeoutMS?
coreClaim: `timeoutMS` defines a client-side operation timeout budget where supported by the driver.
mechanism: CSOT applies a deadline across multiple operation phases rather than only selection.
example: A Node.js driver operation can use timeoutMS to bound the whole client-side attempt.
counterpoint: Support and exact behavior are driver-version-specific.
practicalTakeaway: Use CSOT to align driver work with application deadlines.

title: The Main Knobs Map To Routing, Time, And Resources
learnerQuestion: Which options should I think about together?
coreClaim: Driver knobs group into routing policy, time budgets, and connection resources.
mechanism: Read preference/tags/staleness/localThresholdMS route; timeoutMS/serverSelection/connect/socket bound time; pool options manage resources.
example: A latency-sensitive regional read uses tags plus timeout and pool sizing.
counterpoint: Global defaults can be wrong for mixed workloads.
practicalTakeaway: Tune options by workload class.

title: Connection And Pool Settings Decide Whether Selected Servers Are Usable
learnerQuestion: What can fail after server selection succeeds?
coreClaim: A selected server still needs an available or creatable connection from its pool.
mechanism: CMAP governs checkout, connection creation, pool clearing, max pool size, and wait behavior.
example: High concurrency can wait on pool checkout even with a healthy primary.
counterpoint: Oversized pools can create server load and resource pressure.
practicalTakeaway: Measure pool checkout and connection creation separately from command latency.

title: Network Errors Mutate Topology State, Not Only The Current Operation
learnerQuestion: Why does one network error affect later operations?
coreClaim: Network errors can update server descriptions, clear pools, and wake waiting selectors.
mechanism: SDAM and CMAP react to errors by invalidating state and forcing rediscovery or reconnection.
example: An error marks a server Unknown and clears stale pooled connections.
counterpoint: Not every error has the same topology or pool consequence.
practicalTakeaway: Trace error labels and driver events after network failures.

title: The Driver Preserves Correctness During Primary Failover
learnerQuestion: Why does the driver pause or fail operations during election?
coreClaim: During failover, the driver avoids routing writes until a suitable primary is known.
mechanism: SDAM invalidates old primary state and selection waits or fails until topology updates.
example: A write receives server selection failure while topology is ReplicaSetNoPrimary.
counterpoint: Brief unavailability is preferable to writing to a stale primary.
practicalTakeaway: Design request budgets around expected failover windows.

title: Retries Depend On Selection, Labels, Sessions, And Operation Type
learnerQuestion: Why didn't the driver retry that operation?
coreClaim: Retries depend on operation eligibility, sessions, topology, error labels, and configured retry behavior.
mechanism: Retryable reads/writes specs define eligible operations and conditions.
example: A retryable write may retry after a network error if requirements are met.
counterpoint: Application-level blind retries can duplicate work or amplify outages.
practicalTakeaway: Let driver retry rules inform app retry policy.

title: Drivers Select Routers; Routers Select Shards
learnerQuestion: Does the driver choose shards?
coreClaim: In sharded deployments, drivers select suitable mongos routers; mongos targets shards.
mechanism: Server selection treats mongos servers as operation targets, while cluster routing happens server-side.
example: A driver balances across mongos routers within selection rules.
counterpoint: Read preference and transaction behavior still pass through the driver and command.
practicalTakeaway: Debug router selection separately from shard targeting.

title: Load-Balanced Mode Changes What The Driver Is Allowed To Know
learnerQuestion: How is load-balanced mode different from normal discovery?
coreClaim: Load-balanced mode limits normal topology discovery and relies on serviceId-aware connection behavior.
mechanism: Drivers connect through a load balancer and use load-balanced spec rules instead of discovering all backend servers.
example: Connection pinning and serviceId matter for some operations.
counterpoint: Misusing loadBalanced options can break normal topology assumptions.
practicalTakeaway: Use load-balanced mode only for deployments designed for it.

title: A Server Selection Error Is A Topology Snapshot
learnerQuestion: Why are server selection errors so verbose?
coreClaim: Selection errors often include the driver's current topology description and candidate state.
mechanism: The error captures topology type, server descriptions, RTT, errors, and compatibility state.
example: ReplicaSetNoPrimary with each member Unknown or Secondary explains why writes cannot route.
counterpoint: Error formatting varies by driver.
practicalTakeaway: Preserve full selection error details in logs.

title: Ask Which Filter Removed All Candidates
learnerQuestion: How do I debug no suitable server?
coreClaim: No suitable server means one or more selection filters removed every candidate.
mechanism: Check topology type, server type, operation type, read preference, tags, staleness, latency, compatibility, and pinning.
example: Secondary read with tag set requiring a region that has no healthy secondary.
counterpoint: Network and auth failures may prevent servers from becoming candidates at all.
practicalTakeaway: Debug candidate elimination step by step.

title: A Connection String Encodes Topology Assumptions And Budgets
learnerQuestion: Why can the URI make routing fail?
coreClaim: Connection string options encode discovery mode, replica set name, TLS, load balancing, routing, and timeout budgets.
mechanism: URI options configure SDAM, server selection, pooling, and timeouts before commands run.
example: Wrong directConnection or replicaSet option changes discovery behavior.
counterpoint: Driver defaults differ and change over time; verify with current docs.
practicalTakeaway: Treat the connection string as production configuration.

title: Use Read Preference Intentionally, Not As A Generic Scale Knob
learnerQuestion: Can I send all reads to secondaries to scale?
coreClaim: Read preference changes routing, freshness, failover, and debugging behavior.
mechanism: Read preference modes plus tags/staleness/localThresholdMS decide eligible read targets.
example: Analytics read from tagged regional secondaries with max staleness, while account reads stay primary.
counterpoint: Some workloads require primary reads for freshness or causal expectations.
practicalTakeaway: Define read routing by consistency and UX requirements.

title: Different Failures Call For Different Knobs
learnerQuestion: Which option should I tune for this failure?
coreClaim: Topology, selection, connection, pool, socket, and command failures require different fixes.
mechanism: Map symptom to stage before changing timeout or pool settings.
example: Pool checkout wait is not fixed by increasing serverSelectionTimeoutMS.
counterpoint: Temporary mitigation may differ from root-cause fix.
practicalTakeaway: Tune the failing stage, not the loudest timeout.

title: Drivers Expose Events For The Hidden State Machine
learnerQuestion: How do I see what the driver is doing?
coreClaim: Driver events expose SDAM, CMAP, command, and pool behavior that normal command latency hides.
mechanism: Monitor topology changes, server heartbeat events, pool checkout, connection creation, command started/succeeded/failed, and retry labels.
example: Pool checkout latency explains slow requests before command execution starts.
counterpoint: Event APIs differ across drivers.
practicalTakeaway: Enable driver observability before incidents.

title: Let The Driver Own Topology; Make App Retries Bounded And Observable
learnerQuestion: How should application code work with the driver?
coreClaim: Applications should reuse long-lived clients, avoid manual host routing, and keep retries bounded by explicit budgets.
mechanism: Let SDAM and server selection manage topology while app code sets operation deadlines and observes events.
example: One client per process with timeoutMS and structured retry logging.
counterpoint: Some workflows need business-level retries above the driver, but they must be idempotent and bounded.
practicalTakeaway: Do not fight the driver's topology state machine.

title: Common Ways To Fight The Driver
learnerQuestion: What practices make driver behavior worse?
coreClaim: Manual host pinning, per-request clients, broad secondary reads, ignored tags, command-only latency monitoring, and blind app retries undermine driver design.
mechanism: These practices bypass or obscure SDAM, selection, pooling, and retry behavior.
example: Creating a client per request prevents stable pools and topology state.
counterpoint: There are narrow cases for direct connections, but they should be explicit.
practicalTakeaway: Use driver primitives rather than reimplementing topology logic.

title: Production Checklist For Driver Routing Resilience
learnerQuestion: What should I review before production?
coreClaim: Resilient driver routing requires correct topology config, explicit routing policy, aligned time budgets, and sized pool capacity.
mechanism: Checklist maps to discovery, selection, failure behavior, and resources.
example: Replica set URI with set name, read preference policy, timeoutMS, pool settings, and event logging.
counterpoint: Workload-specific testing is still required.
practicalTakeaway: Review driver configuration as part of architecture review.

title: What The Driver Does For You
learnerQuestion: What is the core mental model?
coreClaim: The driver observes topology, decides suitable servers, and recovers state after failures.
mechanism: Heartbeat monitoring, server selection filters, pool clearing, retry eligibility, and wakeups work together.
example: After network error, the driver updates state and later selects a different suitable server.
counterpoint: Applications must still set budgets and observe behavior.
practicalTakeaway: Think observe, decide, recover.

title: The Hidden State Machine Is The Product
learnerQuestion: Why does this all matter?
coreClaim: The driver state machine abstracts distributed-system movement so applications can issue database operations against a changing deployment.
mechanism: Discovery, selection, pooling, retries, and timeouts convert topology changes into bounded operation behavior.
example: Primary failover becomes temporary selection failure and recovery rather than manual rerouting.
counterpoint: Incorrect configuration can defeat this abstraction.
practicalTakeaway: Let the driver handle topology; make its decisions visible.

title: How To Think About Driver Behavior
learnerQuestion: What should I remember in practice?
coreClaim: Driver behavior is topology-aware routing under explicit time, pool, and read policy constraints.
mechanism: Writes need writable targets; reads use read preference; selection timeout waits for suitability; localThresholdMS/tags/staleness refine candidates.
example: A server selection error can reveal a ReplicaSetNoPrimary state and candidate list.
counterpoint: Do not generalize one language driver's defaults to all drivers.
practicalTakeaway: Use precise vocabulary for routing, timeout, and pool failures.

title: Follow-up Reading
learnerQuestion: Where can I verify the driver behavior?
coreClaim: Driver specifications define cross-driver behavior, while manual and language driver docs define user-facing options.
mechanism: References group SDAM, server selection, CSOT, CMAP, read preference, and connection string options.
example: Use specs for semantics and Node/Go docs for language-specific configuration.
counterpoint: Driver documentation changes; verify current versions before tuning.
practicalTakeaway: Read both the spec and your language driver's current docs.
